title: Purnam adah: full from full
word: then two weeks of the peace chants
hookLine: full from full, and the thunder that tells humans: give
carry: purnam adah: the full gives and stays full
tomorrow: what should get in through your ears first?

cards: Subtract something and you get less. A kid learns that with a plate of cookies and a hungry sibling. This peace chant breaks the rule, and it does it on purpose.
It takes the full from the full, and says the full is what's left. Tradition chants it before the Isha Upanishad, and it is very odd arithmetic to say out loud.

teach.h: PURNAM ADAH: THAT IS FULL, THIS IS FULL.
teach.b: It's known by its first words, purnam adah. In plain words: that is full. This is full.
From the full, the full comes out.
Take the full from the full, and the full alone remains. Then: Om, peace, peace, peace. The same lines open the fifth book of the Brihadaranyaka.
Many readers hear that as Brahman, beyond what the eye sees, and this as the world, or the self, right here. Both full. Not a piece broken off, not a lesser copy.
The schools of Vedanta explain how, each in its own way. And just after it, the same book tells a story. Gods, humans and demons go to their father, Prajapati, and ask to be taught.
To each he says one syllable: da. The gods hear damyata, restrain yourselves. The demons hear dayadhvam, be compassionate.
Humans hear datta: give. You've understood, he says. And the text says the thunder still repeats it: da, da, da.
One way to hear the chant and the story side by side, offered here as a reading: humans are told to give, and the chant before it says giving from the full doesn't leave the full any less.
And daana, giving, is a duty Hindu teaching asks of every home; the Gita says giving should never be given up. So you give from the full, not from what's left over.

how: Purnam adah is chanted as the peace chant of the Isha Upanishad, before and after its study, and it is also widely chanted on its own at the start of prayers and gatherings.

games.q: what does “then two weeks of the peace chants” mean?
o: a vow to give away half of everything you own
a prayer asking to be filled with food and wealth
a chant: from the full, the full; the full remains

games.q: the week's lines. tap the pairs.
p: that is full; this is full

s: purnam adah says the world is a small piece broken off from Brahman
it calls both that and this full; nothing is a smaller piece or a lesser copy.
the same lines also open a section of the Brihadaranyaka
Brihadaranyaka 5.1.1; tradition chants them with the Isha.
in the Brihadaranyaka, Prajapati's one syllable 'da' tells humans: give
gods hear restrain, demons hear be compassionate, humans hear datta, give (Brihadaranyaka 5.2).

games.q: at the temple your little brother asks why dad puts money in the hundi every visit, when 'it just means we have less.' what fits today?
o: it's a fee, so the prayers count.
da: humans are told to give, and the chant says the full remains full.
you should only give once you have extra.
games.why: Prajapati's 'da' tells humans to give, and purnam adah says what comes from the full leaves the full whole. daana is pouring from the full.

practice: If you chant, say purnam adah once, slowly, and the three shantis after it. If you don't pray, think of one thing you could give today: an hour, some help, something you own.
Picture giving it from what's already full in you, not from what's left over, and stay with that picture for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: The peace chants, and today purnam adah: from the full, the full; take the full away, and the full remains.

orig.note: Sanskrit: that is full; the opening words of the Isha's peace chant.

carryVoice: Hold this: purnam adah, the full gives and stays full. Da: give. That's the week.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 5.1.1 (purnam adah purnam idam), chanted as the peace chant of the Isha Upanishad

Bhagavad Gita 18.5 (sacrifice, giving and austerity are not to be given up)
